tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful practice before the recital.
She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.
They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.
Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.
He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Success depends of careful practice before the recital.**

In standard English, depend never partners with of. The locked pattern is depend on (or upon) plus a noun or gerund for the thing that controls the outcome. Here careful practice is that controller, so the satellite must be on.

Mark it wrong and prefer "Success depends on careful practice before the recital."
**B) She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.**

Responsible takes for when you name a duty or job. Responsible of is not an English ownership or duty frame. Keep the gerund watering; only the preposition needs to change.

That duty frame fails — rewrite as "She is responsible for watering the neighbour's plants."
**C) They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.**

As an adjective, interested locks to in: interested in learning or interested in Portuguese. On belongs with focus or concentrate, not with interested. Swap the satellite and the summer-course line becomes native.

Reject this satellite mix-up; the clean version is "They are interested in learning Portuguese this summer."
**D) Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.**

Despite is a single preposition and never takes of. You can write Despite the rain or In spite of the rain — but not Despite of. Either drop of after despite or switch the whole phrase to in spite of.

**Tip:** Despite ∅; in spite of.

Drop the extra of and write "Despite the rain, the picnic went ahead."
**E) He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.**

Accuse (and be accused) locks to of plus a wrongdoing noun or gerund. Here accused of cheating is exactly the exam pattern. Keep of and the -ing form together; nothing else needs fixing.

Keep this: accused of correctly marks the alleged wrongdoing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Before a recital or a neighbour-sitting favour, English often locks a verb or adjective to one preposition — and the wrong partner sounds almost right if you translate from another language.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is all about fixed dependency and responsibility patterns: depend on, responsible for, interested in, despite (no of), and accused of. The classic false friends are of after depend/responsible/despite, and on after interested.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the head word and the preposition right after it. Ask whether that pair is the textbook lock for this meaning. If you can swap in the standard preposition and the sentence suddenly sounds native, mark the original false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.
Her recipe differs of last year's version.
We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.
The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.
She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.**

Insist on plus a gerund is the fixed forcefulness pattern. He insisted on seeing the sheets, not a bare infinitive after insist. The form matches the textbook lock for this meaning.

Accept the line: insist on + -ing is the right forcefulness lock.
**B) Her recipe differs of last year's version.**

Differ compares one thing with another using from. Differs of is a transfer error, not a recognised variant. The recipe line needs from before last year's version.

That comparison fails — rewrite as "Her recipe differs from last year's version."
**C) We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.**

Careful exam English wants apologise for a fault or inconvenience. Apologised about is weaker and often marked wrong even when it turns up in speech. Spilling juice is the fault, so for is the locked satellite.

Mark it wrong and prefer "We apologised for spilling juice on the carpet."
**D) The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.**

Focus and concentrate take on, never to, when they name a topic of attention. Ocean plastics is that topic, so the documentary must focus on it. To after focus is simply the wrong lock.

Focus never takes to for a topic; write "The documentary focuses on ocean plastics."
**E) She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.**

Participate in correctly names involvement in an event or activity. The weekend pottery workshop is exactly that kind of event. The preposition lock matches the meaning, so the line stands.

That works — participated in correctly names workshop involvement.
tasks.solution_overview:
These lines mix everyday insist, differ, apologise, focus, and participate — verbs that almost all students know, but that each demand one locked preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch insist on + -ing, differ from, apologise for, focus on, and participate in. The traps swap of/about/to into slots that English does not allow for those heads.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the verb, then name the preposition that textbooks glue to it. If the sentence uses a different satellite, it is false even when the meaning is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.
The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.
She is good in swimming long distances.
We look forward to meeting your cousins.
He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.
tactical_explanations:
**A) They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.**

Object takes to, not against: objected to the new quiet-hours rule. Protest against is a different verb with a different preposition. Against after object is a classic false friend from other languages.

Reject the false friend; the clean version is "They objected to the new quiet-hours rule."
**B) The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.**

Capable of plus a gerund is the standard ability frame. Handling the front desk fits that slot cleanly. Do not confuse it with able to + infinitive — different head, different pattern.

**Tip:** Capable of doing; able to do.

This is sound — capable of + -ing is the ability frame you want.
**C) She is good in swimming long distances.**

Skills and activities take good at in exam English: good at swimming. Good in is reserved, at best, for school subjects in some varieties, and even there at is safer for a sport or skill. Long-distance swimming is an activity, so at is required.

That skill lock fails — rewrite as "She is good at swimming long distances."
**D) We look forward to meeting your cousins.**

Look forward to is a multi-word unit; to is a preposition here, so it takes a noun or gerund. Meeting your cousins is the correct -ing complement, not a bare infinitive. The cousins line is correctly formed.

Keep this: look forward to + -ing is correctly locked.
**E) He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.**

Succeed in plus -ing reports achievement. Succeeded to repair copies manage to, which is the wrong head for this verb. The bicycle-chain line needs in + repairing, not a to-infinitive.

**Tip:** Succeed in + -ing; manage to + V.

Succeed needs in + -ing, not a to-infinitive — prefer "He succeeded in repairing the bicycle chain."
tasks.solution_overview:
Object, capable, good, look forward, and succeed all look friendly — until the wrong preposition or infinitive slips in after them.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The fixed frames here are object to, capable of + -ing, good at (skills), look forward to + -ing, and succeed in + -ing. Mixing against/in/to-infinitives against those locks is the trap set.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check two layers: which preposition the head wants, and whether what follows should be a gerund rather than a bare or to-infinitive.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.
This jacket belongs to my older brother.
You can rely of her to bring the tent.
They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.
A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.**

Consist of lists the ingredients or parts of something. Consist from has no place in this frame (be made from is a different pattern). Tomatoes, cucumber, and feta are the parts, so of is required.

Mark it wrong and prefer "The salad consists of tomatoes, cucumber, and feta."
**B) This jacket belongs to my older brother.**

Belong to marks ownership cleanly: the jacket belongs to my older brother. Never write belong of for possession. The to satellite matches the ownership meaning here.

Accept the line: belongs to cleanly marks ownership.
**C) You can rely of her to bring the tent.**

Rely, depend, and count all take on for trust. Rely of is the same transfer trap as depend of. Her as the trustworthy person needs on before the infinitive complement.

Rely of fails the trust pattern — rewrite as "You can rely on her to bring the tent."
**D) They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.**

You complain about a problem (noise, service) and complain to a person. Complain for is non-standard for naming the grievance topic. Noisy neighbours upstairs are the problem, so about is the lock.

That grievance frame fails; write "They complained about the noisy neighbours upstairs."
**E) A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.**

Prevent someone from + gerund is the restraint lock. The locked-gate line uses from entering correctly. Do not replace from with to after prevent.

Keep this: prevented them from + -ing is the correct restraint frame.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ownership, composition, trust, complaint, and prevention verbs are tightly glued to one preposition each in everyday English.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Target consist of, belong to, rely on, complain about, and prevent from. Swapping from/of/for into those slots is enough to fail the item.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the preposition names parts, possession, support, a grievance topic, or a blocked action — then match the lock listed above.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.
This trail is similar with the one near the lake.
My playlist is different than yours in every genre.
She has been married with her partner for twelve years.
The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.**

Famous for plus a feature is the standard reputation pattern. Tiled façades fit that slot as a tourist trademark. Famous as would name a role, not a characteristic feature.

That works — famous for correctly names Lisbon's trademark feature.
**B) This trail is similar with the one near the lake.**

Similar, identical, and comparable take to, not with. With after similar is a near-miss that looks plausible but fails the exam lock. The lake trail comparison needs to.

**Trap:** similar with looks close to compare with, but the adjective lock is similar to.

Reject similar with; the clean version is "This trail is similar to the one near the lake."
**C) My playlist is different than yours in every genre.**

In careful exam English prefer different from (or different to in some BrE). Different than is often marked down even where American speech allows it. Playlist comparisons are safest with from.

**Trap:** different than is common in speech but exams usually want different from.

Exam English wants from here — rewrite as "My playlist is different from yours in every genre."
**D) She has been married with her partner for twelve years.**

Married to a person is the lock. Married with copies other languages and belongs instead in frames like live with. Her partner is a person, so to is required.

Married with fails; prefer "She has been married to her partner for twelve years."
**E) The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.**

Afraid of plus a noun (thunderstorms) is correct and natural. Frightened of follows the same of pattern. Night storms sit cleanly in that of slot.

Accept the line: afraid of correctly marks the feared noun.
tasks.solution_overview:
Adjective + preposition pairs feel flexible when you translate, but exam English treats famous for, similar to, different from, married to, and afraid of as closed locks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set checks reputation (famous for), comparison (similar to / different from), marriage (married to), and fear (afraid of). With, than, and from transfers are the usual failures.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the preposition and ask which one the adjective textbooks require. If your guess differs from what is on the page, the sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We arrived to the station just before midnight.
Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.
They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.
Look at the mural behind the café.
We talked the film for almost an hour.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We arrived to the station just before midnight.**

Arrive at a station or building and arrive in a city or country — not arrive to. Get to is the pattern that keeps to for destinations. A station is a point location, so at is the lock.

**Trap:** arrive to copies get to; stations take arrived at.

Arrive to copies the wrong verb — write "We arrived at the station just before midnight."
**B) Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.**

Listen to plus an object is obligatory in standard exam English. Hear can take a direct object; listen cannot. The podcast episode is the object of attention, so to must stay.

Keep this: listen to correctly takes the podcast as object.
**C) They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.**

Wait for someone or something. Wait cannot take the bus as a bare object here. Twenty minutes in the rain still needs for before the bus.

That bare wait fails — rewrite as "They waited for the bus for twenty minutes in the rain."
**D) Look at the mural behind the café.**

Look at directs visual attention to a target. The mural behind the café is that target, and at is the right preposition. Watch can take a bare object; look usually needs at.

This is sound — look at correctly directs attention to the mural.
**E) We talked the film for almost an hour.**

Talk about a topic (or talk to a person). Talk the film drops the required about before the topic. Discuss the film needs no about — different head, different pattern.

**Tip:** Talk about a topic; discuss takes a bare object.

Talk needs about for a topic; prefer "We talked about the film for almost an hour."
tasks.solution_overview:
Arrive, listen, wait, look, and talk are easy verbs — and easy to strip of the preposition English still needs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch arrive at/in (not to), listen to, wait for, look at, and talk about. Dropping the satellite or using the wrong one after movement and perception verbs is the test.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the verb can take a bare object in standard English. If it cannot, restore the missing preposition before you decide true or false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She goes to work by foot every morning.
They travelled to the coast by train.
The match starts in Monday evening.
I usually read in night when the house is quiet.
We met on a cold Friday afternoon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She goes to work by foot every morning.**

Walking uses on foot, not by foot. By is for vehicles: by bus, by train, by car. The morning commute on foot keeps on, the walking exception.

**Tip:** By + vehicle; on foot.

By foot is the wrong means lock — rewrite as "She goes to work on foot every morning."
**B) They travelled to the coast by train.**

By train correctly names the means of transport. The coast journey uses the default by + vehicle lock. Nothing else in the line fights that pattern.

Accept the line: by train correctly names the means of travel.
**C) The match starts in Monday evening.**

Days and dated evenings take on: on Monday or on Monday evening. In Monday is wrong; in the evening is fine only without a weekday. Monday evening is a dated time slot, so on is required.

Days take on, not in — prefer "The match starts on Monday evening."
**D) I usually read in night when the house is quiet.**

At night is the fixed time phrase. Bare in night is not standard. In the night is rarer and shaded differently; the quiet-house reading wants at night.

Mark it wrong and write "I usually read at night when the house is quiet."
**E) We met on a cold Friday afternoon.**

On plus a day or date phrase is standard: on a cold Friday afternoon. The adjective cold sits inside the noun phrase and does not change the preposition lock. Everyday and exam English both accept this shape.

Keep this: on + dated day/time phrase is correctly formed.
tasks.solution_overview:
Time and transport prepositions are closed sets: English picks by, on, in, or at by rule, not by feel.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember by + vehicle, on foot (the walking exception), on + day/dated time, and at night. In Monday and in night are classic calendar false friends.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Classify each phrase as transport means or time slot, then apply the closed-set rule instead of translating from another language.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.
Don't blame me about the burnt toast.
Thanks for helping me move the sofa.
The hostel provided us with clean towels.
Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.**

Congratulate someone on an achievement. For after congratulate is weaker and typically marked wrong in exams. Winning the baking contest is the achievement, so on is the lock.

Congratulate locks to on — rewrite as "We congratulated her on winning the baking contest."
**B) Don't blame me about the burnt toast.**

Blame someone for something. About does not replace for after blame. Accuse of is a different head — do not import its satellite onto blame.

**Tip:** Blame for / accuse of.

Blame of/about fails here; prefer "Don't blame me for the burnt toast."
**C) Thanks for helping me move the sofa.**

Thanks for plus a gerund or noun is the correct gratitude frame. Helping me move the sofa fits that for slot cleanly. Thank someone for doing X follows the same for lock in full-sentence form.

That works — thanks for + -ing is the gratitude pattern you want.
**D) The hostel provided us with clean towels.**

Provide someone with something is the classic ditransitive lock. Clean towels fit that with complement. Provide something to someone is another acceptable shape; with is right here.

Accept the line: provided us with correctly supplies the towels.
**E) Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.**

Charge someone with an offence. Of belongs to accuse, not to charge. Vandalising the bus stop is the charged offence, so with is required.

**Trap:** charge/accuse near-synonyms do not share satellites — charge with, accuse of.

Charge shares no satellite with accuse — write "Police charged him with vandalising the bus stop."
tasks.solution_overview:
Speech-act and legal-ish verbs look alike when someone blames, thanks, or charges — but each head keeps its own preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate congratulate on, blame for, thank for, provide with, and charge with. Mixing for/of/about across those heads is the designed trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify the speech act first, then recall its private preposition. Near-synonyms do not share satellites.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.
She is fond from old jazz records.
They take pride of their community garden.
I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.
He gets bored of the same playlist every day.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.**

Keen on plus a noun or gerund expresses enthusiasm, in the same neighbourhood as interested in. Early-morning runs along the canal fit that on slot. The canal-run line is correctly locked.

Keep this: keen on correctly marks the enthusiasm frame.
**B) She is fond from old jazz records.**

Fond of names people or things you like. Fond from is never the pattern. Old jazz records need of after fond.

Fond from fails — rewrite as "She is fond of old jazz records."
**C) They take pride of their community garden.**

Take pride in an achievement. Pride of mixes the noun pride with the adjective proud of. Their community garden needs in after take pride.

**Trap:** proud of invites of, but take pride locks to in.

Take pride wants in, not of; prefer "They take pride in their community garden."
**D) I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.**

Tired of plus a gerund or noun is fixed for weariness with a situation. Waiting for the plumber fits that of slot. Exhausted from effort is a different idea with a different preposition.

This is sound — tired of + -ing correctly marks weariness with the wait.
**E) He gets bored of the same playlist every day.**

Careful English prefers bored with (or by). Bored of is informal and often marked non-standard in exams. Fed up with is the of-cousin — do not import of onto bored for this playlist line.

**Trap:** bored of is common informally, but exams usually want bored with.

Exam preference is bored with — rewrite as "He gets bored with the same playlist every day."
tasks.solution_overview:
Attitude words — keen, fond, pride, tired, bored — each lock to one preposition, and near-synonyms refuse to share.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold keen on, fond of, take pride in, tired of, and bored with. From/of swaps and informal bored of are the failure modes.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Memorise the pair as a single chunk. If a synonym would take a different preposition, do not import that preposition onto this head.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.
We stayed home because of the flooding.
She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.
In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.
As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
**A) According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.**

According to plus a source is the reporting phrase. According with is not used for this meaning. The weather app is the source, so to is correctly locked.

Accept the line: according to correctly cites the weather app.
**B) We stayed home because of the flooding.**

Because of plus a noun phrase correctly gives a reason for staying home. The flooding fills that noun slot. Because + clause would need a finite clause, not of.

**Tip:** Because of + noun; because + clause.

That works — because of correctly marks the reason noun phrase.
**C) She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.**

Instead of coffee is the comparison lock. Bare instead cannot take a following noun this way. As an adverb, instead stands alone; before a noun you need instead of.

**Trap:** dropping of after instead is an easy chunk error — restore instead of.

Instead needs of before the alternative — write "She chose tea instead of coffee after dinner."
**D) In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.**

In addition to stretching pairs with as well as — both keep to, not of. Of after addition is a despite-style transfer onto the wrong chunk. Stretching needs to after in addition.

**Trap:** in addition of looks like in spite of, but the lock is in addition to.

In addition of fails; prefer "In addition to stretching, he iced his knee."
**E) As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.**

As a result of plus a noun phrase is the fixed causal chunk. The delay fills that noun slot and explains missing the opening act. As a result alone needs a comma and a following clause, not of + noun dropped.

Keep this: as a result of correctly marks the causal noun phrase.
tasks.solution_overview:
Multi-word prepositions are all-or-nothing chunks: miss or swap the final preposition and the whole phrase collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set locks according to, because of, instead of, in addition to, and as a result of. Stripped of/to after instead and addition are the main traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each opener as a fixed string. If the last word of the chunk is missing or wrong, mark false without rewriting the rest of the clause.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.
The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.
Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.
Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.
He specialised in marine biology at university.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.**

Insist that plus a clause is a valid frame alongside insist on + -ing. Leaving before dawn is correctly embedded under that. Both frames are fine; they are just different shapes for different complements.

**Tip:** Insist that (clause) vs insist on (gerund).

This is sound — insist that + clause is a valid alternative to insist on + -ing.
**B) The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.**

Discourage someone from swimming, not to swim. The from + -ing pattern matches prevent and keep. After dark swimming needs from + swimming after discourage.

**Trap:** to-infinitive after discourage looks like encourage to, but discourage takes from + -ing.

Discourage never takes to — rewrite as "The coach discouraged them from swimming after dark."
**C) Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.**

Recover from an illness is the standard medical collocation. Recover of is wrong. Warm soup helping him recover from the cold uses the right lock.

Accept the line: recover from correctly names the illness source.
**D) Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.**

For prevention, stop someone from finishing (or stop someone finishing). Stop her to finish means pause in order to finish — the wrong reading for blocking the marathon. Nothing will stop her needs from + finishing here.

**Trap:** stop to do ≠ stop from doing — to here reads as purpose, not prevention.

Stop to do is purpose, not prevention; prefer "Nothing will stop her from finishing the marathon."
**E) He specialised in marine biology at university.**

Specialise in a field is fixed. Marine biology at university fits that in lock. The subject line needs no other satellite.

Keep this: specialised in correctly names the university field.
tasks.solution_overview:
Some verbs invite an infinitive that is actually illegal — they want from + -ing, or a that-clause instead.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep insist that (alongside insist on), recover from, and specialise in. Catch discourage and preventive stop, which take from + -ing rather than to-infinitives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When a verb seems to take to + V, pause: is it really a prevent/encourage family member that wants from + -ing? Check that family first.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm used to waking up before sunrise.
She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.
They are accustomed with long bus rides.
He prefers walking to cycling in the city.
We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'm used to waking up before sunrise.**

Be/get used to plus a gerund means accustomed to a habit. Waking before sunrise fits that familiarity frame. I'm used to waking is the present-habit reading, not past used to + base verb.

That works — be used to + -ing correctly marks the familiar habit.
**B) She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.**

Past habit needs used to + base verb: used to wake, not used to waking. Do not confuse this with be used to + -ing for present familiarity. When she worked nights is a past-habit setting, so the bare infinitive wake is required.

**Trap:** used to waking mixes past-habit used to with the be used to + -ing pattern.

Past-habit used to wants a bare infinitive — rewrite as "She used to wake up before sunrise when she worked nights."
**C) They are accustomed with long bus rides.**

Accustomed to mirrors used to for familiarity. Accustomed with is wrong. Long bus rides need to after accustomed.

Accustomed with fails; prefer "They are accustomed to long bus rides."
**D) He prefers walking to cycling in the city.**

Prefer X to Y correctly stacks two options: walking to cycling. That to comparison is the standard exam shape. Than would belong to rather, not prefer.

Accept the line: prefer A to B correctly compares walking and cycling.
**E) We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.**

Prefer … than is not the English comparison. Use prefer walking to cycling, or would rather walk than cycle. Rainy-day preferences keep to after prefer, not than.

**Trap:** prefer … than imports rather than's satellite onto the wrong head.

Prefer … than imports the wrong satellite — write "We prefer walking to cycling when it rains."
highlights: used to waking up before sunrise when
tasks.solution_overview:
Used to and be used to look like the same phrase; prefer … to/than collides the same way. This task forces you to keep the frames apart.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate past-habit used to + base verb from be used to + -ing, keep accustomed to, and compare with prefer A to B — never prefer … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask first whether used to means past habit or present familiarity. Then check prefer comparisons for to versus than.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.
In spite the heat, they finished the hike.
Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.
She refrained to comment during the argument.
Please refrain from posting spoilers online.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite of plus a noun phrase equals despite. The of is part of the chunk, and the hike line keeps it. Despite the heat would also work — despite drops of; in spite keeps it.

**Tip:** In spite of keeps of; despite drops it.

Keep this: in spite of correctly includes the required of.
**B) In spite the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite must be followed by of before a noun. In spite the heat is an incomplete chunk. Insert of and the contrast phrase matches despite.

**Trap:** dropping of from in spite of is a near-miss of the full multi-word preposition.

Missing of breaks the chunk — rewrite as "In spite of the heat, they finished the hike."
**C) Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.**

Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase with no extra of, like despite. The late start fills that bare noun slot. The choir line is correctly formed without of.

This is sound — notwithstanding + noun needs no of.
**D) She refrained to comment during the argument.**

Refrain from commenting, not refrain to comment. Abstain follows the same from + -ing shape. During the argument, the restraint frame wants from + commenting.

**Trap:** to-infinitive after refrain copies refuse to; refrain locks to from + -ing.

Refrain copies refuse to here; prefer "She refrained from commenting during the argument."
**E) Please refrain from posting spoilers online.**

Refrain from plus a gerund is the fixed restraint pattern. Posting spoilers fits that from slot. Keep from after refrain; a to-infinitive would break the same head as the previous false line.

Accept the line: refrain from + -ing correctly blocks the spoiler posting.
tasks.solution_overview:
Contrast markers and restraint verbs look interchangeable until you notice which ones keep of and which ones refuse it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Despite and notwithstanding take a noun with no of; in spite of needs of. Refrain takes from + -ing, not a to-infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For contrast phrases, check whether of is required or forbidden. For refrain, demand from + -ing every time.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.
Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.
She has no intention to cancel the trip.
There is no point of arguing about the score.
What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?
tactical_explanations:
**A) The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.**

Depend on correctly ties the outcome to temperature. Outcome of X and depend on Y can both be right in one sentence. Experiment outcome and temperature condition use their private locks side by side.

That works — depends on correctly links outcome to temperature.
**B) Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.**

Access to a place is the fixed pattern for entry rights. Access of is not used for places. The roof terrace after dusk keeps to for that entry meaning.

Keep this: access to correctly names entry rights to the terrace.
**C) She has no intention to cancel the trip.**

Have no intention of cancelling is the preferred exam lock. Intention to is often marked wrong even when heard elsewhere. Cancelling the trip needs of + -ing after intention.

**Trap:** intention to looks like a future infinitive, but exams prefer intention of + -ing.

Intention to is the exam near-miss — rewrite as "She has no intention of cancelling the trip."
**D) There is no point of arguing about the score.**

No point in arguing is the frame here. Point of arguing mismatches this no-point structure, though what's the point of is a related pattern. Match the whole fixed frame: there is no point in + -ing.

**Trap:** of after no point mixes what's the point of with there is no point in.

No point of mixes frames; prefer "There is no point in arguing about the score."
**E) What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?**

What's the point in staying matches an acceptable rhetorical frame with in + gerund. Point in and point of both appear; match the whole fixed question shape. If the museum is closed, staying is the pointless gerund under in.

Accept the line: what's the point in + -ing is an acceptable fixed question frame.
tasks.solution_overview:
Abstract nouns — outcome, access, intention, point — each pick a locked preposition that does not follow from "future" intuition alone.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep depend on and access to. Prefer intention of + -ing and match point in/of to the whole fixed frame; bare intention to is the soft trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Do not assume to after every noun that looks ahead. Check the collocation dictionary pattern for that noun before judging.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.
He was angry about the cancelled ferry.
They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.
I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.
We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.**

Angry with a person plus for a reason is a solid double pattern. With her brother names the person; for borrowing the headphones names the offence. Both locks can sit in one sentence without conflict.

**Tip:** Angry with people; about situations; for a reason.

This is sound — angry with … for correctly splits person and offence.
**B) He was angry about the cancelled ferry.**

Angry about a cancelled ferry correctly targets a situation or event, not a person. If the complement were a sibling or colleague, you would switch to angry with. The ferry cancellation is a situation, so about is right.

Keep this: angry about correctly targets the cancelled-ferry situation.
**C) They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.**

Pleased with or by — not pleased of. Proud of is the of-cousin; do not import it onto pleased. The surprise birthday brunch needs with or by after pleased.

**Trap:** proud of invites of, but pleased locks to with/by.

Pleased of fails — rewrite as "They were pleased with the surprise birthday brunch."
**D) I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.**

Delighted with a result is natural and grammatical. Delighted by also works; delighted to hear that… is another frame. How the garden turned out is a result, so with fits.

Accept the line: delighted with correctly marks pleasure at the garden result.
**E) We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.**

Surprised by or at the news — not surprised from. From after surprised is a transfer that does not belong to this emotion adjective. Sudden snowfall needs by or at.

**Trap:** from after surprised looks causal but the lock is surprised by/at.

Surprised from is the wrong causal satellite; prefer "We were surprised by the sudden snowfall."
tasks.solution_overview:
Emotion adjectives split people from situations, and they reject of/from transfers that proud sometimes invites.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Use angry with for people and angry about for situations; keep pleased/delighted with and surprised by/at. Pleased of and surprised from are the traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the complement is a person or a situation, then lock the preposition. Reject of/from unless the adjective truly owns them (proud of, not pleased of).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
This jacket smells like woodsmoke.
She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.
Can you remind me of locking the back door?
Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.**

Taste of a flavour is the fixed sensory pattern for substances in the soup. Smell of works the same way for a substance. Garlic and lemon fill that of slot as flavours present in the soup.

That works — tastes of correctly names the flavours in the soup.
**B) This jacket smells like woodsmoke.**

Smell like for resemblance is acceptable and grammatical here. Smell of woodsmoke would also work as a substance reading. Woodsmoke as a comparison keeps like in this jacket line.

**Tip:** Of for substance; like for resemblance.

Keep this: smells like correctly marks resemblance to woodsmoke.
**C) She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.**

Remind someone of a person or thing triggers memory or resemblance. My primary-school teacher is that memory or resemblance trigger. The of satellite is correct for this reading.

Accept the line: reminded me of correctly marks memory or resemblance.
**D) Can you remind me of locking the back door?**

For a future action, remind me to lock — not remind me of locking. Of would suggest memory or resemblance, not a prompt to act. Locking the back door is an instruction, so to + base verb is required.

**Trap:** remind of vs remind to — of is memory; to is a future prompt.

Remind of locking mixes memory with a future prompt — rewrite as "Can you remind me to lock the back door?"
**E) Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.**

Remind someone to plus an infinitive correctly issues a prompt about a future action. Bring the picnic blanket is that instruction reading. Of would be for memory or resemblance, not for "bring the blanket."

This is sound — remind him to correctly issues the future-action prompt.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sensory of/like patterns are usually safe; remind is the hard verb because it splits into two different frames.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Taste of and smell like are fine for flavour and resemblance. Remind of covers memory or resemblance; remind to covers a future prompt — do not mix them.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For remind, ask whether the complement is a memory trigger or an instruction to act. That single question chooses of versus to.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.
Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.
The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.
Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.
Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.**

Owing to plus a noun phrase is a formal because-of equivalent. High winds fit the causal slot for cancelling the festival. The full chunk keeps to before the cause noun.

Keep this: owing to correctly marks the formal causal phrase.
**B) Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.**

Owing needs to before the noun phrase. Bare Owing the… is an incomplete multi-word preposition. Insert to and the festival cancellation reason is restored.

**Trap:** stripping to from owing to is a classic chunk scar — restore Owing to.

Owing without to is a chunk scar — rewrite as "Owing to the high winds, the festival was cancelled."
**C) The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.**

Due to plus a noun is widely accepted as a causal preposition in modern exam English. It matches because of for this postponed-hike reading. Flooding on the trail fills that noun slot, so the line stands.

Accept the line: due to correctly marks the cause of the postponement.
**D) Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.**

Due the flooding drops the required to. Like owing to, due to is a fixed chunk that fails without its final preposition. Restore to before the flooding noun phrase.

**Trap:** Due the… is the same missing-to error as Owing the… — both need to.

Due the… drops the required to; prefer "Due to the flooding, the hike was postponed."
**E) Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.**

Thanks to plus a noun credits a (usually positive) cause. A clear sky and the meteor shower fit that favourable shade. The to satellite is part of the fixed chunk and must stay.

**Tip:** Thanks to (often positive); owing/due to (neutral or negative).

That works — thanks to correctly credits the clear sky as cause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Causal multi-word prepositions all keep a final to: strip it and the phrase is broken even if the nouns are clear.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Owing to, due to, and thanks to are complete only with to. Owing the… and Due the… are automatic fails; the full forms with to are true.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for owing/due/thanks and confirm the next word is to. Missing to alone decides false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She accused him for leaving the gate open.
They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.
He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.
The club banned him from using the tennis courts.
Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She accused him for leaving the gate open.**

Accuse someone of doing, not for. For belongs to blame. Leaving the gate open is the alleged act, so of is required after accuse.

**Trap:** blame for vs accuse of — near-synonyms that refuse to share satellites.

Accuse shares blame's for by mistake — rewrite as "She accused him of leaving the gate open."
**B) They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.**

Suspected of plus a gerund is the fixed collocation for alleged wrongdoing. The same of satellite appears after accuse; do not swap in for here. Feeding the stray cats fits that of + -ing slot.

Keep this: suspected of correctly marks the alleged act.
**C) He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.**

Convicted of an offence is the standard legal and exam pattern. For appears in loose usage, but of is the safer lock here. Trespassing on farmland is the offence, so of is required.

**Trap:** convicted for is heard, but exams prefer convicted of (charge with is different).

Exam English wants convicted of — prefer "He was convicted of trespassing on farmland."
**D) The club banned him from using the tennis courts.**

Ban someone from plus a gerund or noun is correct. Prohibit follows from; forbid someone to is a different shape. Using the tennis courts is blocked with from after banned.

Accept the line: banned him from + -ing correctly marks the prohibition.
**E) Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.**

Compensate for a loss. In this sense compensate cannot take the loss as a bare object. The old oak's loss needs for before the noun phrase.

Compensate needs for before the loss; write "Nothing can compensate for the loss of the old oak."
tasks.solution_overview:
Fault, suspicion, conviction, bans, and compensation are preposition-heavy: one wrong satellite and the legal flavour collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold accuse/suspect/convict of, ban from, and compensate for. Accuse for, convict for, and bare compensate the loss are the designed errors.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pair each verb with its private preposition before you care about the gerund. Dropping or swapping that satellite fails the item.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.
Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.
She prides herself in finishing every crossword.
She takes pride in finishing every crossword.
He is proud for his daughter's science prize.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent on plus a noun or gerund matches depend on for conditions. Dry weather this weekend fills that condition slot. The plan's dependency uses on, not of.

This is sound — contingent on correctly marks the weather condition.
**B) Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent of is a depend-of style transfer. The condition lock after contingent is on. Approval waiting on dry weather needs that on satellite.

**Trap:** of after contingent copies depend of — both heads want on.

Contingent of copies the depend-of trap — rewrite as "Approval is contingent on dry weather this weekend."
**C) She prides herself in finishing every crossword.**

Pride oneself on doing, not in, after the reflexive verb. In belongs to take pride in. Finishing every crossword needs on after prides herself.

**Trap:** take pride in invites in onto pride oneself, which actually locks to on.

Pride oneself locks to on, not in; prefer "She prides herself on finishing every crossword."
**D) She takes pride in finishing every crossword.**

Take pride in plus a gerund is fixed and correct here. Finishing every crossword fits that in slot. Be proud of is the adjective cousin with of — different head, different satellite.

**Tip:** Take pride in / be proud of / pride oneself on — three different locks.

Keep this: take pride in correctly marks pride in the achievement.
**E) He is proud for his daughter's science prize.**

Proud of an achievement, not proud for. His daughter's science prize needs of after proud. For after proud is a false friend from other languages.

Proud for fails — rewrite as "He is proud of his daughter's science prize."
tasks.solution_overview:
Pride frames look identical until you notice the verb under them: pride oneself, take pride, and be proud each want a different preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Contingent follows depend → on (never of). Then separate pride oneself on, take pride in, and be proud of — importing in/for across those frames fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the exact verb phrase first. Only then pick on, in, or of. Contingent always tracks depend on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.
The café had run out from cups before noon.
I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.
She objects to being photographed without consent.
He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.
tactical_explanations:
**A) By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.**

Run out of plus a noun is the depletion pattern. Cups before arrival fit of after run out. By the time we arrived sets the past perfect depletion reading cleanly.

Accept the line: run out of correctly marks depleted cups.
**B) The café had run out from cups before noon.**

Run out from cups is wrong; materials take of after run out. From does not replace of for supplies. Before noon, the café still needs run out of cups.

Run out from fails the depletion lock — rewrite as "The café had run out of cups before noon."
**C) I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.**

Looking forward to the hike, not for. To is part of the multi-word verb and takes a noun or -ing. The weekend hike is that noun complement under to.

**Trap:** for after look forward copies wait for; the chunk is look forward to.

Look forward for copies wait for; prefer "I'm looking forward to the weekend hike."
**D) She objects to being photographed without consent.**

Object to plus a gerund is correct: objects to being photographed. Against is a false friend from other languages. Without consent is the setting; the satellite after object stays to.

That works — objects to + -ing correctly marks the objection.
**E) He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.**

Succeeded in repairing, not on. On belongs to insist, not succeed. The leaky tap needs in + repairing after succeeded.

**Trap:** succeeded on imports insist on onto the wrong head — succeed locks to in.

Succeed on imports the wrong head's satellite — write "He succeeded in repairing the leaky tap."
tasks.solution_overview:
Close with the high-frequency exam cluster: run out, look forward, object, and succeed — each fails or passes on one satellite preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Lock run out of, look forward to, object to, and succeed in. From/for/on swaps are the only difference between true and false here.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore how natural the sentence feels in translation. Match the exact multi-word verb to its textbook preposition, then decide.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
